This Guy Has Been Working for Ford for 60 Years, Has Tools Older Than His Workmates
8 photos
Photo: Ford From the Road
The first time Eddie O'Brien walked through the gates of the Ford Dagenham plant, back in 1966, he was a 16-year-old apprentice. Fast forward to 2026, and he has just celebrated 60 years with the company with no interruption whatsoever.
Eddie O'Brien has been with Ford through 13 different Prime Ministers. Back when he started, England had just won the World Cup, something it has not done again since. The world has changed over the years, but one thing has remained the same. Eddie showed up for his shift, day or night.
His own celebration in 2026 coincides with a major anniversary for his workplace. The event that marked his six-decade-long career with Ford took place exactly 95 years after the Ford Dagenham site started operating.
Dagenham is now a major powertrain hub, producing high-volume diesel engines, such as the 2.0-liter EcoBlue, for Ford’s global commercial vehicle lineup. But for 71 years, the manufacturing facility was a massive vehicle assembly facility, rolling out over 11 million cars, trucks, and tractors, including models such as the Cortina , Capri, and Fiesta. Vehicle assembly officially ceased at the site in 2002, when the final UK-built Ford Fiesta rolled off the production line.
Photo: Ford From the Road For him, the Blue Oval adventure started with the Ford Trade School, doing what they called a sandwich course. At the time, he actually applied for three jobs. One was at a rubber factory in Essex, and another was with British Gas. But he wanted to work for Ford the most, so here he is, 60 years later.
He began training at the specialized company trade school located in nearby Harold Hill. Upon entering the main Dagenham complex, he was first deployed to the River Plant. He later transitioned to the facility’s Central Repair Garage to sharpen his mechanical expertise.
In 1973, he found his permanent home within the company. For over five decades, he has worked specifically as a Mechanical Maintenance Craftsman. His primary responsibility has been maintaining the massive infrastructure required to handle vehicle logistics, keeping heavy industrial machinery, site tugs, and locomotives running smoothly.
Many refer to the machine shop where he spends most of his time as "Eddie's Shop." It is where he does his job and has tools older than some of his current workmates. He bought them himself ages ago. He remembers that he paid 5 pounds for a micrometer to gauge small distances and thickness. That was a week’s wages at the time. He remembers he and his colleagues were paid in cash back then.
Photo: Ford From the Road There are photos of him in black and white up on the walls, showing different stages of his career. Eddie credits his incredible work longevity in a demanding blue-collar career to his lifetime dedication to physical health, particularly his love for cycling and taking part in charity bike rides. He took up cycling about 24 years ago and hasn't stopped since.
He only wished he'd started sooner. If he had, he would have ridden more than the few 100-mile races that he has completed so far. He still does it, usually in the company of one of his sons outdoors or by himself, indoors. " I do like to push it, get my blood pumping ," he says.
He also takes his grandchildren cycling every once in a while. Staying active is probably one of the reasons he hasn't gained weight over the years. He also took up running ten years ago but had to stop after he injured his foot.
He is well aware that now, his time at Ford is inching closer to the end due to the physical demands of the job and admits that " 60 years is a nice number to sign off on ." " I think some of the younger guys do look after me a little bit. Not too much, " he says.
Photo: Ford From the Road The best part of his job? He got to work on and for some iconic vehicles. For instance, he had to make jigs for some repairs for the Le Mans Ford GT40 at the Heritage Center as fast as he could because they needed them for a TV show. As a reward, he received a plaque with one of the pistons from the blow-up engine on it.
He has been a Ford owner over all these years. He drives a Fiesta now, but he has had Cortinas, other Fiestas, and even Transits, along with a Sierra, which he affectionately calls his favorite. However, he has always been in love with motorcycles. He has even raced them until 1988. He has recently sold his Kawasaki 500 Enduro that he used to ride to work every day, regardless of the weather. All of a sudden, he no longer enjoyed it, so he got rid of it.
Once he retires, he plans to focus on cycling and spending time with his family, especially with his grandchildren and great-grandchildren. He wasn't even planning to start a family in the near future when he started working for Ford.
